turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Sorry we're late, doctor. The 42 just sat there in the rain and then my brolly turned inside out, honestly.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're fine, come on in, both of you. Grim old morning for May.

[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Grim is the word. And that waiting room tea, I had a cup, well I wouldn't give it to the plant, and the pink wafers, I can't do pink wafers since that do at my sister's, not that she's ill or anything, she just buys the wrong biscuits.
[SEG0004] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Sit down before you tell him your whole week.
[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): I'm sitting, I'm sitting. These chairs are lower than they look, mind, and my knees don't love the drop.
[SEG0006] person_4 (NURSE): I'll slip the numbers in before I go. Blood pressure today is 148 over 86, pulse 76. Tuesday's bloods are on the screen when you want them.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's helpful. What have you come in for, then?
[SEG0008] person_3 (PATIENT): It's the diabetes I'm worried about, and those kidney numbers on the letter. That's why we're here, not the bus and not the tea.
[SEG0009] person_4 (NURSE): Creatinine is 156, eGFR forty-one. I'll get out of your way.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): So, creatinine 156, eGFR 41. Lower than we want. Tell me, in your own time, what you actually take each day.
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): Right, well, I line them up on the blue tray, not the green one, the green one is for the post. Amlodipine five milligrams in the morning for the pressure.

[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I never miss that one. Then the cholesterol one at night, atorvastatin twenty milligrams, and the sugar tablets, that's metforman, uh, metformin, five hundred milligrams with breakfast and five hundred with my tea.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me say that back. Amlodipine five in the morning for the pressure, atorvastatin twenty at night, metformin five hundred twice a day.

[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. I couldn't tell you the proper name of it, it's just that powder, a small spoon in warm water, nothing else from the health shop.
[SEG0015] person_1 (CAREGIVER): You haven't said the ramipril yet.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): I was coming to it. Ramapril, uh, ramipril, five milligrams in the morning, same swallow as the amlodipine. They were very clear I keep taking it.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, and we'll keep the ramipril at five milligrams each morning. What about painkillers, anything from the shop?
[SEG0018] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Ibuprofen. I've said it till I'm blue in the face.

[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): It's for the knee, that's all. The two hundred milligram tablets, two of them, three times a day. The knee itself has been three months, the right one, it grinds on the stair.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Three times a day is a lot. With this kidney reading I don't want ibuprofen anywhere near you.
[SEG0021] person_3 (PATIENT): If I don't take them I can't get down the bottom step, it catches, and then I have to sort of go sideways, and the rail is loose, I keep meaning to...
[SEG0022] person_1 (CAREGIVER): The rail's not the doctor's problem.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll deal with the pain in a minute. Any swelling of the ankles?
[SEG0024] person_3 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. They're slim as ever, I can still see the bones, I check when I put the cream on.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain?
[SEG0026] person_3 (PATIENT): No chest pain at all. Not when I walk, not when I sit, nothing, and I would notice because I think about these things.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath?
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Not breathless either. The paper shop is up a little slope and I do that fine, it's only the knee that makes me slow, not my wind.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Waterworks or bowels, any change there?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): No change. No stinging when I go, bowels every morning after porridge, you don't need the timetable but it's reliable, has been for years.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Can I look at your ankles while we talk?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Course. Shoes off, the laces are a fiddle, double knot, my father always said double knot and I've never...
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are a bit puffy, and it pits when I press. Right a touch more than the left.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Does it? Well, actually, by the evening they do come up. I loosen the laces. I didn't think it counted, because by morning they've gone down again.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that evening swelling been going on?
[SEG0036] person_1 (CAREGIVER): Sorry, the phone, no I'll silence it. His niece texted about a sofa, of all things.
[SEG0037] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Worse if I'm on my feet, and if I put them up on the stool it eases. Right one more, like you said.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): So the swelling is two weeks, worse on your feet, better with the legs up, and it settles overnight. You said no at first, but this fuller picture fits what I can see.
[SEG0039] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, that's fair. I wasn't trying to hide it, I just, the letter about the kidneys was the thing in my head, the number 41, I kept reading that line.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. The knee, right knee, aching three months, worse on the stair. And you've been taking shop ibuprofen against the advice we gave you before.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes. Against advice, I know. Two of the two hundred milligram tablets, three times a day. The box is in my coat even now.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): I need you to stop the ibuprofen from today. It can push the creatinine up, especially with the ramipril and an eGFR of 41, on top of the diabetes and the chronic kidney disease.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Stop it from today. Alright. I'll bin the box when I get in, not the cupboard, the cupboard is how it creeps back.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. Ramipril stays, five milligrams every morning. For the knee I'll prescribe paracetamol, one gram by mouth, up to four times a day, for the next two weeks.

[SEG0045] person_3 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, one gram, four times. I can remember that. Not with the ibuprofen, instead of, and the others stay, the pressure one, the night one, the sugar ones, the powder.

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): The Ayurvedic powder, small spoon each morning, I'll note you're taking it. You can't name the product and neither can I from that, so don't increase it, but I'm not changing it today.

[SEG0047] person_3 (PATIENT): I won't increase it. Same spoon, the blue-handled teaspoon, not heaped, warm water, before the tablets so it doesn't sit on them. My neighbour started me on it, not a doctor, I should say that.

[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): My impression, and it's only a working one, is that the kidney figures have dipped, creatinine 156 and an eGFR of 41, most likely from the ibuprofen on the background of the chronic kidney disease. I wouldn't want to stamp a new diagnosis until the bloods are repeated.

[SEG0049] person_3 (PATIENT): So it might come back up if I stop the ibuprofen. I hope so. I've been careful with the sugar, truly, the porridge, no biscuits except that pink one today which was a mistake, and I walk when the knee allows.
[SEG0050] person_2 (DOCTOR): Walking is fine so long as the knee tolerates it. I'll book a repeat kidney blood test, creatinine and eGFR, before I see you again.
[SEG0051] person_1 (CAREGIVER): When's that, then? He needs it written down or it won't happen.

[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Six weeks, in clinic, with me. The blood test a few days before that visit. Reception will book both on your way out. Come sooner if the ankles get worse, or you're not passing water, or you feel very unwell.

[SEG0053] person_3 (PATIENT): Six weeks, bloods a few days before, bin the ibuprofen, paracetamol instead, ramipril stays. And I'll tell you if the ankles blow up. Thank you, doctor, and sorry again about the time.
[SEG0054] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're welcome. Nothing to be sorry for. See you in six weeks.

spec.situation: Older diabetic with kidney disease on review; creatinine and eGFR read aloud; takes ibuprofen from a shop against advice; ramipril continued, painkiller advice changed.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

bad.reason: Ibuprofen stopped today is supported; dose detail wrong: transcript says 400 mg per dose, not 200 mg.
bad.text: ibuprofen (dose=200 mg, frequency=two tablets three times a day, indication=knee pain, status=discontinued, reported_by=doctor)

bad.reason: Creatinine result is given, but no requester for the completed test is stated.
eGFR result is given, but no requester for the completed test is stated.

Negative finding missing: patient initially denied ankle swelling when asked.
